clue.text: Pain in the neck if it invades blood

indicators.note: an invader pushes inside territory, so one piece goes into the middle of another

parts.note: gore is shed blood
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grumble that something is a nuisance if it gets into the bloodstream.
explanation.walkthrough: GO(IT)RE: 'Pain in the neck' reads as the idiom for a nuisance, but here it is literal.
explanation.definitionFit: A goitre is a swollen thyroid gland, a literal affliction located in the throat.

clue.text: Butter and spread written up in good English

indicators.note: in a down entry, writing something upwards means reading it from bottom to top

parts.note: a ram butts with its head, so it is a butter
short for margarine, a spread

explanation.surface: Instructions about butter and margarine, written in proper English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butter' looks like the dairy product but is one who butts. RAM + MARG read upwards gives GRAMMAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar is the set of rules for correct language, so good English is a fair loose synonym.

clue.text: Animal disease caught by extreme Italian dramatist

indicators.note: something caught is held inside whatever caught it
extreme parts are the two ends, so only the first and last letters count

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word
bovine spongiform encephalopathy, mad cow disease

explanation.surface: An Italian picks up a disease from an animal.
explanation.walkthrough: BSE sits between the ends of Italian: I(BSE)N.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen was the Norwegian playwright of A Doll's House and Hedda Gabler.

clue.text: Performance of highly questionable American movement?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a rendering of a song or piece
second meaning: the US practice of transferring suspects to other countries for interrogation

explanation.surface: A dubious show staged by an American movement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extraordinary rendition' was the controversial US practice of secretly moving detainees abroad.
explanation.definitionFit: A rendition is a performance of a work, and also the covert transfer of prisoners between countries.

clue.text: Places, we hear, for steak and chips

definitions.text: Places, we hear, for steak and chips

parts.words: Places, we hear, for steak and chips
parts.note: surface reading: restaurants serving a classic meal of beef and fried potatoes
setter's reading: 'steak' sounds like stake, a bet, and chips are gambling tokens

explanation.surface: Somewhere to get a steak dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'We hear' applies to 'steak' only: say it and it becomes the wager, and chips become gaming counters.
explanation.definitionFit: Gambling halls are where people place stakes using chips as tokens.

clue.text: Brown medal found in ancient city

indicators.note: something found in a place lies within it

parts.note: Ur was a city of ancient Mesopotamia
Member of the Order of the British Empire, a British honour

explanation.surface: Archaeologists find a bronze-coloured medal in an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: U(MBE)R. The MBE is a British honour given with a medal.
explanation.definitionFit: Umber is a natural earth pigment of dark brown colour.

indicators.note: letters set free are no longer held in their order and can be rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: The title of a song whose theme is the cry of liberation 'I'm free!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Theme of' reads as one phrase, but 'of' belongs with the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A leitmotif is a recurring musical or literary idea associated with a character or subject.

indicators.note: whatever carries something holds it within itself

parts.note: refuse as a noun means rubbish
H is the map abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to bring a walking cane to hospital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb but is the noun, rubbish. T(H)RASH.
explanation.definitionFit: To cane someone is to beat them with a stick, which is to give them a beating.

parts.note: a male is referred to as he
to wing is to fly

explanation.surface: Instructions for a fisherman: cast the fly over the cut.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'over' means the man's piece sits above the flying piece, not that something is finished.
explanation.definitionFit: Hewing is chopping with an axe, so it is cutting in the sense of felling or shaping.

parts.note: surface reading: people who haven't signed up, as for an electoral roll
setter's reading: people not marked present when the register is called, because they are not there

explanation.surface: People who never got round to registering, perhaps to vote.
explanation.walkthrough: A school register is the roll call; those who don't answer it are missing.
explanation.definitionFit: People absent from class or work are not recorded as present when the roll is taken.

indicators.note: an entrance is a way in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: to bar is to block or prevent
the postal abbreviation for Rhode Island, a US state

explanation.surface: A rose bush planted to stop people getting into a state building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' looks like the verb 'got up' but is the flower. B(RI)AR.
explanation.definitionFit: Briar is a name for a wild or dog rose, a thorny climbing shrub.

clue.text: Australian Embassy returns part of bridge

indicators.note: returning means going back the way one came, so the letters are read backwards
only a part of the words is taken, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: the letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: An Australian embassy returns some part of a bridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'part of' does double duty, signalling the hidden letters and also the definition. The Menai Bridge crosses the Menai Strait to Anglesey in Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Menai is the first word of the Menai Suspension Bridge's name, so it is literally part of that bridge.

indicators.note: playing with something means toying with it, mixing its parts around

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is fun, or perhaps just acting the clown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing the fool' is the idiom, but 'playing' is the signal and 'the fool' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An ignoramus is an ignorant, foolish person, so the noun matches a dunce or simpleton.

clue.text: "Compiler, thy gun repair", as written by De la Mare?

definitions.text: as written by De la Mare

indicators.note: repairing something means taking it apart and putting it back together, so the letters are reassembled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A mock-poetic command to the setter to fix a gun, as a poet might phrase it.
explanation.walkthrough: Walter de la Mare was an English poet; 'repair' rhymes with 'Mare', so the quoted line and the poet's name form a rhyming pair.
explanation.definitionFit: A poet such as de la Mare writes in pairs of lines that end in matching sounds.

parts.note: the Duke of York, a royal title
a shire is a heavy draught horse breed

explanation.surface: A nobleman sitting on his horse hands out dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: Yorkshire pudding is a savoury batter baked in the oven, served with British roast beef dinners; 'pudding' leads away from dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Yorkshire is a type of batter pudding, the name standing alone for the dish.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to drug someone into calm

explanation.surface: A slangy exchange: someone asks about drugs and gets an enthusiastic reply.
explanation.definitionFit: To dope is to drug into calmness, and a calm composed person is unhurried and dignified.

indicators.note: broadcasting scatters seed widely, so the letters are scattered into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone hurries off to listen to a radio programme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' looks like a verb of hurrying, but 'the runs' is slang for the illness. British spelling has -OEA.
explanation.definitionFit: The runs is colloquial for a stomach upset with loose bowel movements.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: kinds or makes of product
second meaning: marks with a hot iron, as cattle

explanation.surface: A postal worker arranging stamps.
explanation.definitionFit: Brands are kinds of goods, and to brand is to burn an identifying mark onto something.

parts.note: a rough plan or outline drawing

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so only the first letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A loose scheme for nurturing a youthful leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'young leader' reads as a youthful boss but means the word's first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sketchy is rough and lacking detail, just as a vague account is.

parts.note: f, forte, is the musical direction for loud
an earful is a long telling-off

explanation.surface: Someone frightened of a noisy dressing-down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scared of' reads as one phrase but 'of' is just the join.
explanation.definitionFit: Fearful means full of fear, so it is a synonym for frightened.

clue.text: Note: a moth flying has six feet

parts.note: F is a musical note

indicators.note: something flying flutters about, so its letters move into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An entomologist's note: a moth in flight has six legs.
explanation.walkthrough: Insects have six legs, so 'six feet' points to legs; it is really the measure.
explanation.definitionFit: A fathom is a unit of water depth equal to six feet.

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: leery means wary or suspicious
CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: Doubts about a partner's promiscuity.
explanation.walkthrough: LE(CH)ERY: the 's on companion's is the join to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Lechery is excessive sexual desire, which is lustful wantonness.

parts.note: a miniskirt
O is round in shape
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A short skirt worn by a new servant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skirt round' looks like 'avoid' or a container signal; here 'round' is just the circle letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A minion is a subservient follower or underling who carries out orders.

parts.note: in means fashionable
to press forward as a crowd does

indicators.note: without a heart the middle goes, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: The tabloids are callous but not seditious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartless' seems to describe the press, but it acts on 'not', taking its middle out.
explanation.definitionFit: An insurgent person or group is rising in revolt against authority.

parts.note: REM sleep, the rapid eye movement phase
'with' joins IT on

explanation.surface: A suggestive proposition met by a shocked 'Pardon?'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pardon' looks like 'what did you say?' but is the verb to forgive.
explanation.definitionFit: To remit a sin or debt is to cancel it, which is what forgiving it means.

clue.text: Priest enters church with this, perhaps

definitions.text: Priest enters church with this, perhaps

indicators.note: to enter is to go inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: RC stands for Roman Catholic church
Eli is the priest in the Old Testament book of Samuel

explanation.surface: A priest processes into church carrying something.
explanation.walkthrough: R(ELI)C: the whole clue also describes the answer, as a priest might carry a saint's remains into a Catholic church.
explanation.definitionFit: A relic is a venerated object, such as a saint's bone, carried in religious processions.

indicators.note: something collared is grabbed and held, so it ends up surrounded

parts.note: lard is pig fat
the crossword setter refers to themselves as I

explanation.surface: A crossword setter is seized by a corpulent landowner.
explanation.walkthrough: LA(I)RD. A laird is a Scottish landowner.
explanation.definitionFit: A laird owns a landed estate in Scotland, so he is a landowner who lets land to tenants.

indicators.note: regular means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth, eighth and tenth letters

explanation.surface: A personal ad: a man named Regular is told to go and find a widow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mr Regular' reads as a person's name, but 'Mr' is fodder and 'Regular' the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom is a fixed phrase whose meaning isn't deducible from its words.

clue.text: King embraced by clown lied about animal

indicators.note: someone embraced is held within another's arms

parts.note: Coco was a famous circus clown
R for rex, Latin for king

indicators.note: about can mean all around or turned about, so the letters are moved around

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A clown hugs a king and then lies about some animal.
explanation.walkthrough: CO(R)CO + an anagram of LIED. Coco the Clown was a famous Bertram Mills circus performer.
explanation.definitionFit: A crocodile is a large aquatic reptile, a kind of animal.

indicators.note: a reflection shows things mirror-image, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a neon is a lamp or light
a try is an attempt or test

explanation.surface: A warning sign forbidding some experiment with reflected light.
explanation.walkthrough: NEON reads the same forwards apart from the swapped middle: backwards it is NOEN, then TRY.
explanation.definitionFit: A no entry sign is a traffic or door notice that forbids access.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the first of May, written day before month as in Britain, a spring holiday
second meaning: the international radio distress call

explanation.walkthrough: '1/5' looks like a fraction, one fifth, but it is a date written day/month in the British way, so it means the first of May.
explanation.definitionFit: May Day is the traditional spring festival on the first of May, and mayday is the distress call used by ships and aircraft.
